idea:
# Idea to refine: a shared grocery list for a two-person household

One list, two phones, no friction: either person adds an item in a couple of taps,
and whoever is in the shop sees it immediately and can tick it off.

Non-negotiables (do not design these away):
- It must work with no account, no login and no sign-up of any kind.
- It must stay a single HTML file with no build step and no package install.
- It must never send the list to a server; the data stays on the two devices.

What I want from the refinement: make this genuinely usable for two people who
shop separately, while keeping all three non-negotiables intact.

hits.critique: This is the first version. The previous draft went over the length limit, so this one is shorter but keeps the same content. Two problems remain. First, the owner's brief says the shopper 'sees it immediately', but without a server the two phones can't update each other live, so this version only promises an honest 'last synced' time. Second, when a person sends the update link through a messaging app, the list passes through that app's servers. That needs the owner's ruling against O-3.
hits.version:
# Pocket List: a shared grocery list in one HTML file

One HTML file, opened from any static host or from the home screen. There is no account. The list lives only in each phone's local storage, and the app never sends it to a server.

**Add and tick:** one field (Enter adds the item) and tap to tick. Ticked items move to "got it", and one tap brings them back.

**Merge, never overwrite:** each item has an ID and an edit time. When the phones sync, the newest edit to each item wins and deletions are remembered, so both phones end up with the same list.

**Sync without a server:**
1. **Together:** Phone A shows a QR code with the list after the `#` in the link. Phone B scans it and the lists merge. Browsers never send the `#` part to the host.
2. **Apart:** "Send update" makes the same link. The person sends it with a messaging app of their choice, and one tap on it merges the list. The app itself contacts no server.

**Honest timing:** each phone shows "last synced with partner: 14:02". Nothing claims to be live.
changes: Cut the version to under 1011 characters and kept every feature
Made clear that the person chooses the messaging app and the app itself contacts no server
open_questions: Is it acceptable for the update link to go through a messaging app like WhatsApp or Signal, or should sync happen only with the phones together (QR code)?
Would you accept a 'last synced' time instead of truly immediate updates?

owner_conflicts.item: Brief: 'whoever is in the shop sees it immediately'
owner_conflicts.reason: O-3 and O-1 rule out a relay server, so live updates between phones that are apart aren't possible. The closest honest option is fast manual sync plus a visible 'last synced' time.

owner_conflicts.item: O-3: never send the list to a server
owner_conflicts.reason: Sending the update link through a messaging app means the list passes through that app's servers. The app itself never contacts a server, but the owner should confirm this is acceptable.

decisions.text: P-1: Sync goes through a link with the list after the # (QR code when together, any messaging app when apart). Edits merge per item, the newest edit wins, and deletions are remembered.
P-2: The app never claims to be live and always shows the last time it synced with the partner.

hits.critique: The QR approach preserves the constraints, but messaging a list-bearing link violates O-3. One-way scanning also cannot make both lists converge when both people edited them. Wall-clock timestamps risk incorrect merges, and ‘last synced’ implies agreement that receiving one snapshot cannot establish. Immediate remote updates remain unresolved.
hits.version:
# Pocket List
One self-contained HTML file, no build or packages, no account, login or sign-up. Store the list on each phone; never send it to a server. Include all code locally.

**Shopping:** type and Enter to add; tap to tick. Completed items move to ‘got it’; tap to restore. Changes save locally immediately.

**Exchange:** when together, show a QR link containing the snapshot after `#`; the partner scans and merges it. Then scan their merged snapshot back. For larger lists, use numbered QR chunks and merge only once all arrive. Never share these links through messaging, email or cloud storage: those services receive the list. Clear the fragment after importing.

**Merge:** give items random IDs and edits logical counters with a device-ID tie-breaker; the highest version wins. Keep deletion records so old snapshots cannot resurrect items. Concurrent edits converge, but one can lose; independently added duplicates remain separate.

**Honest status:** show ‘last update received’ and ‘changes since last exchange’, never ‘live’. Shopping separately means using the last exchanged list; additions cannot appear immediately without another exchange. Clearing browser storage loses that phone’s copy; a partner snapshot can restore it.

Use a stable HTTPS address to load the file; phone file-opening support must be tested.
changes: Removed messaging transport because it sends list data to servers.
Made synchronization a two-way exchange with chunking for large snapshots.
Replaced wall-clock ordering with deterministic logical versions.
Distinguished receiving an update from confirmed synchronization.
Made separate-shopping limitations and local-storage loss explicit.
open_questions: Is exchanging updates in person before separate shopping acceptable, given that immediate remote updates remain unavailable in this design?
Which two phone/browser combinations must support the HTML file?

decisions.reason: Messaging transports violate O-3; one-way snapshots do not ensure convergence, and wall-clock ordering is unreliable.
‘Last synced with partner’ overstates what an unacknowledged snapshot proves; retain the prohibition on claiming live updates.

decisions.text: Exchange snapshots directly through two-way QR scanning; support numbered chunks and prohibit server-mediated sharing.
Merge per-item logical versions with deterministic device-ID ties and retained deletion records.
Show last received update and local changes since exchange; never claim live synchronization.

hits.critique: Codex's version fixed real problems. It dropped messaging as a transport, made the exchange two-way, and replaced wall-clock times with logical versions. Five things were still weak or missing. (1) It still put the list in a URL after `#` and only said to clear it after import. If someone scans that code with the phone's system camera, the list lands in browser history, and possibly in history sync. A scanner built into the app avoids this, but the version never said that QR decoding must be part of the file. (2) It said to use a stable HTTPS address but never said why: the camera only works on secure pages. It also didn't explain why this still meets O-3: the host only delivers the code and never receives list data. (3) It didn't mention that iOS Safari can wipe storage after 7 days, which is a real data-loss risk for a list that must stay on the phones. (4) Deletion records were kept forever, and there was no rule for when to remove them. (5) The everyday use was thin: no undo for a wrong tick and no way to clear ticked items. Duplicate items were noted but nothing helped the user deal with them.
hits.version:
# Pocket List
One HTML file with all code inside, including QR drawing and decoding. No build, no packages, no account. The list lives on each phone and is never sent to a server.

**Hosting:** served from a static HTTPS address, because cameras only work on secure pages. The host delivers the code only; no list data ever goes back to it. Add it to the home screen (on iOS this avoids Safari's 7-day storage wipe). The app also asks the browser to keep its storage permanently.

**Use:** type an item and press Enter to add it. Tap to tick, with a 5-second undo. Ticked items move to 'got it'. 'Clear got it' deletes them.

**Swap:** both people tap Swap. Each phone shows its QR code and scans the other's with the in-app scanner. Order doesn't matter, because merging gives the same result either way. Data is compressed. Large lists use numbered QR parts and merge only once all of them arrive. Never use the system camera or a messaging app.

**Merge:** each item has a random ID and a counter. The device ID breaks ties. The highest counter wins. Deletions are recorded so old data can't bring items back. A record is removed once the partner's swap shows they have it too. Two separate edits to one item can mean one is lost. If both people add 'milk', it shows twice and the app offers to combine them.

**Status:** shows 'last swap: Tue 18:04' and 'N changes not yet swapped'. Never shows 'live'.

**Apart:** nothing moves between phones without a swap. Habit: swap before anyone leaves the house.

**Backup:** exports a file to the device. Importing it merges like a swap.
changes: Cut the version to fit within the length limit
QR codes no longer contain a URL with the list after #; the in-app scanner prevents browser-history leaks
QR encoding and decoding are inside the file
Explained the reason for HTTPS and why the host never sees list data
Added home-screen install and a permanent-storage request against iOS's 7-day wipe
Deletion records are removed once the partner's swap shows they have them
Added a 5-second undo, 'Clear got it' and a prompt to combine duplicates
Added local file export and import as a backup, merged like a swap
open_questions: Is a swap only when both people are together acceptable? Items added while you are apart can't reach the shopper. Doing that would need a network relay, which O-3 forbids.
Who hosts the static HTTPS file: the owner, or a free static host?
Should quantities or notes per item be in scope?

decisions.text: QR codes are scanned only with the in-app scanner, never the system camera; the list is never put in a URL.
Served from a static HTTPS address and installed to the home screen; the app asks for permanent storage.
A deletion record is removed once the partner's swap shows they have it too.
Local file export and import as a backup, merged like a swap.

hits.critique: The everyday controls and embedded QR scanner are strong. But swaps converge only if both export frozen snapshots; counters must advance beyond received versions. Deleting acknowledged tombstones lets old backups resurrect items. ‘Last swap’ implies more than receipt proves, and home-screen installation cannot guarantee durable storage. Immediate updates while apart remain incompatible with the permitted transport.
hits.version:
# Pocket List
One self-contained HTML file, including QR encoding/decoding: no build, packages, account or login. List data stays on the two phones; no server receives it.

Open at a stable static HTTPS address for camera access. The host serves code only. Offer home-screen installation and request persistent storage where supported; neither guarantees against data loss.

Type an item and press Enter. Tap to tick, with 5-second undo. Ticked items move to ‘got it’; ‘Clear got it’ deletes them. Duplicate names stay separate, with an option to combine.

Before either person leaves, swap: both tap Swap, freezing their outgoing snapshots, then scan each other’s codes using the embedded scanner. Finish both directions before editing again. Use compressed, numbered QR parts; merge only a complete snapshot. Codes contain data, never URLs. No system-camera or messaging transport.

Items have random IDs. Each edit uses a logical counter above every counter seen; device ID breaks ties. Highest version wins, so concurrent edits to one item can lose one change. Keep deletion records permanently so older snapshots and backups cannot resurrect items.

Show ‘last update received’ and ‘local edits since outgoing snapshot’, never ‘live’ or an unverified sync claim.

When apart, phones cannot exchange updates: each shows only what it already holds. Immediate remote updates are unavailable under these constraints.

Export/import local backup files, merging by the same rules. Keep backups on these devices, outside cloud-synced storage.
changes: Freeze both outgoing snapshots to make a completed two-way swap converge.
Specify counter advancement after receiving versions.
Retain deletion records to protect against stale backups.
Replace ambiguous swap status with receipt and outgoing-snapshot status.
Qualify storage durability and restrict backups to device-local storage.
open_questions: Is exchanging updates only when together acceptable for your separate shopping trips?

decisions.text: P-10: Freeze both outgoing snapshots before scanning; complete both directions before further edits.
P-11: Each local edit advances beyond every observed logical counter.

decisions.reason: Partner acknowledgement does not prevent an older backup from resurrecting a deleted item; retain tombstones.

decisions.text: P-12: Storage persistence is best effort; backups must remain outside cloud-synced storage on the two devices.
